title: Google unveils new TSMC based AI chip variants as cloud demand surges
author: hist78
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Google introduced two versions of its artificial intelligence computing systems on Monday, expanding its chip portfolio as rising demand for AI infrastructure fuels growth in its cloud business.

The systems, called TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, extend Google’s eighth generation of tensor processing units. They strengthen the Alphabet subsidiary’s effort to compete with Nvidia by offering hardware tailored to specific workloads, including confidential computing and applications that process large volumes of information.

The announcement comes as Google’s custom chips become an increasingly important commercial business. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.71 billion in the September quarter, with TPU sales making a meaningful contribution, according to Alphabet. Its shares rose more than 3% in early trading.

TPU 8tx targets governments and regulated industries handling sensitive information. It combines Google’s existing TPU technology with AMD processors to protect data and model weights while they are being processed. Google says the system can cut latency by up to half compared with TPU 8t, with almost no performance penalty from its security features.

TPU 8i Max addresses the memory demands of advanced AI applications. By placing two TPU 8i chips in one package, Google says it doubles computing capacity, on-chip memory and high-bandwidth memory bandwidth. The configuration is intended to help AI agents handle extensive software codebases, video and other demanding tasks.

Both products are new system configurations built around existing silicon, rather than entirely new chip designs. That approach allows Google to adjust memory, networking and security more quickly as customer requirements change.

Bloomberg reported that the variants will become available next year. Their arrival underscores a broader shift toward specialized AI infrastructure, as companies seek systems that balance speed, security, memory capacity and operating costs while supporting increasingly complex applications across a growing range of business and research settings.
